If not, and you throw yourself upon my forbearance and the mercy of those whom you have grievously wronged, take your place in that chair without a word. It has stood waiting for you these two full days.”

Monks murmured something unintelligible, but remained irresolute.

“You must decide promptly,” said Mr. Brownlow. “One word from me, and this choice is lost for ever.”

The man continued to hesitate.

“I have no wish to bargain,” Mr. Brownlow said, “and, representing the most precious interests of others, I have no right to do so.”

“Is there—” Monks asked, his tongue faltering, “is there—no middle way?”

“None.”

Monks glanced anxiously at the old gentleman; but finding only sternness and resolution in his face, he entered the room, shrugged his shoulders, and sat down.

“Fasten the door from outside,” Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, “and return when I ring.”

The men did as they were ordered, leaving the two alone.

“This is fine treatment, sir,” said Monks, flinging down his cloak and hat, “from the oldest friend my father had.”

“It is because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,” answered Mr. Brownlow; “because the hopes and desires of my happy youthful years were entwined with him, and with that lovely creature of his own blood who returned to her God so young, leaving me solitary and alone; because, while still a boy, he knelt beside me at his only sister’s death-bed on the morning when—had Heaven not decreed otherwise—she would have become my young wife; because from that hour my wounded heart held fast to him through every trial and error until his death; because old memories and attachments filled my heart, and the very sight of you recalls thoughts of him; it is for all these reasons that I am inclined to deal gently with you now—yes, Edward Leeford, even now—and to blush at the unworthiness of the man who bears that name.”

“What has the name to do with anything?” the other asked, after watching his companion’s emotion partly in silence and partly in stubborn bewilderment. “What does the name mean to me?”

“Nothing,” Mr. Brownlow replied, “nothing to you. But it was hers; and even after all these years it revives in me, old as I am, the warmth and thrill I once knew at merely hearing a stranger pronounce it. I am exceedingly glad that you have changed it—exceedingly—exceedingly.”

“This is all very fine,” said Monks, to keep his assumed name, after a lengthy silence in which he had shifted jerkily to and fro in sulky defiance, while Mr. Brownlow sat with his hand covering his face.

I would gladly describe all this, and much more, in detail. But to put it briefly, I must have my reward. I long to return to my family and home. Before I provide any further information, and in view of the knowledge I can offer on many important areas of physical and metaphysical science, I must ask your honorable body to use its influence to obtain a pardon for me. My crime was causing the deaths of my creditors when I left Rotterdam. That, then, is the purpose of this document. The person carrying it is an inhabitant of the moon whom I persuaded, and properly instructed, to act as my messenger to earth. He will await your Excellencies’ decision and return to me with the pardon, if it can possibly be obtained.

“I have the honor to remain, etc., your Excellencies’ most humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

When he finished reading this extraordinary document, Professor Rub-a-dub reportedly dropped his pipe on the ground in sheer surprise. Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk removed his spectacles, wiped them, and put them into his pocket. Then, forgetting both himself and his dignity, he spun around on his heel three times in complete astonishment and admiration. There was no question about it: the pardon must be secured. At least, that was what Professor Rub-a-dub swore with a hearty oath, and what the distinguished Von Underduk finally decided too. Taking his fellow scientist’s arm, he started home as quickly as possible, without a word, to consider what steps they should take. But when they reached the mayor’s door, the professor dared to point out a difficulty. The messenger had chosen to disappear—no doubt terrified by the fierce appearance of Rotterdam’s citizens. A pardon would therefore be little use, since nobody but a man from the moon would attempt so distant a journey. The mayor agreed with this observation, and that ended the matter. It did not, however, end the rumors and speculation. Once published, the letter produced all kinds of gossip and opinions. A few people who thought themselves especially wise even made themselves ridiculous by dismissing the entire affair as a hoax. But I believe “hoax,” with people of this sort, is simply a general word for anything beyond their understanding. For my part, I cannot imagine what evidence they base such an accusation on. Let us examine what they say:

With these cries, many of the women, driven into a blind frenzy, spun around, hitting and clawing at their own friends until they fainted from the force of their emotions. Only the men who belonged to them kept them from being trampled.

Even so, not a moment was wasted—not a moment! This Foulon was at the Hôtel de Ville and might be released. Never, if Saint Antoine remembered its own suffering, humiliation, and injuries! Armed men and women poured out of the district so swiftly, pulling even these last remnants after them with such force, that within fifteen minutes Saint Antoine held no living soul except a few old women and the crying children.

No. By then they were all crowding the Hall of Examination, where the ugly, wicked old man stood, and spilling into the open space and streets nearby. The Defarges, husband and wife, the Vengeance, and Jacques Three were at the front of the press, close to him inside the hall.

“Look!” cried Madame, pointing with her knife. “Look at the old villain tied with ropes. How well they did to fasten a bundle of grass to his back! Ha, ha! That was well done. Let him eat it now!” She tucked her knife beneath her arm and clapped as though watching a play.

The people immediately behind Madame Defarge explained her delight to those behind them, who passed the explanation to others, and they to still others, until the neighboring streets rang with applause. In the same way, throughout two or three hours of droning speech and the sifting of countless bushels of words, Madame Defarge’s frequent signs of impatience were echoed far away with astonishing speed. This happened all the more readily because some men, with extraordinary agility, had climbed the building’s outer stonework to look through the windows. They knew Madame Defarge well and relayed signals between her and the crowd outside.

At last the sun climbed high enough to cast a gentle beam, like a promise of hope or protection, directly onto the old prisoner’s head. Such favor was unbearable. In an instant the barrier of dust and chaff, which had held surprisingly long, scattered to the wind, and Saint Antoine had seized him!

The news reached the farthest edges of the crowd immediately. Defarge had only just vaulted a railing and a table and gripped the wretched man in a deadly embrace; Madame Defarge had only just followed and twisted her hand into one of his binding ropes; the Vengeance and Jacques Three had not yet reached them, nor had the men at the windows swooped into the hall like birds of prey from high perches, when the cry seemed to rise throughout the whole city: “Bring him out!”
